The goal with this document is to walk you through setting up your remote development environment for this course. Here we will learn basic navigation in VSCode, later on the day we learn same steps in command line.


## 1. Connect to Remote Server in VS Code
1. Open VSCode, install the Remote Development extension \

Open Extensions (click the icon that looks like four small squares with one detached or press Ctrl+Shift+X / Cmd+Shift+X). Search "Remote - SSH" by Microsoft and install it.

2. Make sure SSH is set up on your machine

  Windows: Settings > Apps > Optional Features > OpenSSH Client \
  Mac/Linux: usually built-in


3. Open the Remote-SSH connection panel \

Look at the bottom-left corner of the VS Code window — there's a small green (or blue) rectangular icon that looks like two arrows facing each other (><). This is the "Open a Remote Window" button. Click it, or use the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P — command bar at the top). \ Select "Connect to Host..." from the menu that pops up.

4. Enter the connection details
Choose "Add New SSH Host," type:

`ssh username@login01.lisc.univie.ac.at`

**Don't forget to replace** ```username``` **with your own lisc username!**

Confirm the SSH config file to save to.

5. Connect and authenticate \

Pick your host from the list. A new VS Code window opens (you'll see it as a separate window/tab). Confirm the fingerprint if prompted, then enter your password/passphrase.

6. Wait for VS Code Server to install \

Watch the bottom-right notification popups for progress. Once done, the bottom-left icon updates to show the host name you're connected to (e.g., "SSH: myserver").

7. What login looks like the second time \

The next time you connect, it will be much faster: click the same "Open a Remote Window" icon, choose your host from the list, and enter your permanent password when prompted. You won't see the fingerprint confirmation again, and VS Code Server is already installed on the cluster, so there's no install.

## 2. Prepare Your Workspace

1. Adjust Your Workspace

Keep the Explorer open in the left sidebar, and open the integrated Terminal via View > Terminal (or Ctrl+`/Cmd+`). You can toggle the whole sidebar on/off with View > Appearance > Show Activity Bar.

Bonus: you can change VS Code's color theme by opening the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P) and typing "Color Theme", or with the shortcut Ctrl+K Ctrl+T (Cmd+K Cmd+T on Mac).

2. Open your work folder 

Use File > Open Folder (top menu), or the folder icon in the Explorer view (the top icon in the left sidebar, looks like two overlapping documents/pages).

Paste this path to our course folder:
 **PROVIDE PATH HERE** 

## 3. Organize Your Project Folder

Before running any analysis, it helps to agree on a folder structure so results, scripts, and logs don't end up scattered. For this course we'll use the structure below — each stage gets its own numbered folder so the order is obvious at a glance, and `scripts/`, `logs/` and `run_log.md` sit alongside them for things that apply across stages:

```text
genome_assembly_project/
|-- 01_qc/
|-- 02_assembly/
|-- 03_evaluation/
|-- 04_annotation/
|-- scripts/             # job scripts and code you write
|-- logs/                # output/error logs produced by your jobs
`-- run_log.md          # manual log: what was run, when, why, parameter choices
```
**Exercise: create this structure**

1. In the Explorer sidebar, right-click your course folder and select "New Folder" to create `genome_assembly_project/`. Open it.
2. Inside it, use "New Folder" again to create folder: `01_qc/`, we'll use it next time.
3. In the main directory right-click and select "New File" to create `run_log.md`. This is your running log of what you did, when, and why — start today's entry now:

```text
## 2026-09-07
- Set up VS Code remote connection to LiSC
- Created genome_assembly_project/ folder structure
```

Keep adding to this log throughout the course — it's the one place to check what you ran and why, especially useful when troubleshooting later.

**WELL DONE!**

## 5. Setting Up Your Working Folder

Within your course scratch directory, make one folder per project, using the following structure:

```raw_data``` — a folder containing symbolic links to (or, rarely, actual copies of) raw data files

```[name of your GitHub repository]``` — your cloned GitHub folder (set up in Section 6 below); this is where you will take daily notes and develop code, with GitHub providing version control

```[analysis folder, e.g. MAFFT]``` — one folder per analysis or piece of software, used to store large intermediate files. If files are small (under 50 Mb), you can keep them inside the GitHub folder instead.

This creates a copy of your repository inside your current directory. You should now see a new folder named after your repository, containing the files from GitHub (including your ```README.md```).

Move into that folder and set your identity for this and future commits:

```text

git config --global user.email "[your email]"
```

**Minimal GitHub cheatsheet:**

```text
git clone URL         move a repository to your current location
git status             see what has changed since your last commit
git add .              stage all changed files to be committed
git commit -m "message"    save staged changes with a description
git push               send committed changes to GitHub
git pull               fetch and merge changes from GitHub
```
